source.title: Protein Language Model Predicts Mutation Pathogenicity and Clinical Prognosis
source.authors: Xianglin Liu; Xinyu Yang; Linkun Ouyang; G. Guo; Jin Su; Ruibin Xi; Ke-Fei Yuan; Fa-Jie Yuan

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. There is an internal inconsistency in the ESM-1 scale results: the text gives a four-value series including 0.874, while Table 2 lists three ESM-1 sizes and assigns 0.874 to ESM-1b.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares mutation-prediction performance across protein-model sizes and reports that larger models do not consistently perform better. This challenges predictable downstream scaling, though it does not test language-model pretraining loss laws.
record.gate_note: The study measures AUC for zero-shot protein-mutation pathogenicity prediction across model sizes. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or test architecture-shape effects. Survival results and comparisons not varying model size do not test the listed versions. The study also reports a masking comparison, but that is not a scale comparison.
record.test_reason: The study compares zero-shot pathogenicity AUC across sizes within three protein-LM families (ESM-1, ESM-2, ProGen2). It argues explicitly that larger models are not always better, which bears on V6 in a protein-sequence setting. It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power laws and tests no extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that protein-LM size is not proportional to pathogenicity-prediction performance. They say ESM-1 and ESM-2 peak near 650M and then decline, and attribute this to likely undertraining given limited protein data, citing Hoffmann et al. ProGen2 is best at 6.4B. Caveat: the claimed ESM-1 decline rests on a text series that includes 0.874, which Table 2 assigns to ESM-1b. Table 2's own ESM-1 values rise monotonically, so only ESM-2 clearly shows the decline. The authors also conclude that BERT-like models suit the task better than generative ones.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates zero-shot protein mutation pathogenicity prediction across pretrained protein-model sizes, using AUC rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies by model family and input masking; the reported ESM-2 results peak at 650M and decline at larger sizes.
record.problems: The outcomes are downstream pathogenicity AUCs rather than held-out pretraining loss. The model-size series are limited, uncertainty estimates are not reported, and the ESM-1 text and table differ in attribution and series length for the 0.874 result.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the masking results of ESM-1b and ESM-1v, EVE, ESM-MSA, or the cancer-survival analysis: these do not report a scale comparison that bears on the tested version. The ESM-2 15B masked entry is not reported as a value.

untested.parts: Whether downstream performance tracks pretraining loss. Whether gains are predictable, since no fit or extrapolation is made. Scaling in data or compute rather than parameters. Tasks other than pathogenicity AUC. No uncertainty estimates are given.
Not tested; no held-out loss is reported.
No power-law form for loss is examined in the protein modality.

missing.what: Qualitative claim that models trained on larger datasets predict better (ESM-1v vs ESM-1b, same 650M size: 0.909 vs 0.874). It bears on V6 via data scale but has no per-dataset-size series.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche T5 is kept because the authors argue explicitly against monotone downstream gains with size. T3 (new setting) would also be defensible. Point estimates come without uncertainty, and the ESM-2 differences above 650M are small (about 0.01–0.02 AUC). They come from 2279 variants across 20 genes, so the challenge is weak. The ESM-2 15B masked value is not reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute changes.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies protein models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in another modality or training regime.
It measures downstream pathogenicity-prediction AUC across model sizes, but does not relate downstream performance to pretraining loss or test other downstream tasks.
No exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared, and the study does not investigate fitting choices or curve shapes for pretraining loss.
